answer.answer: The hardest part is not the screen. It is knowing what the person is trying to do when the screen is in the way, and noticing the moment they hesitate. I do not have a last screen I shipped and watched someone use. When I build an interface, what I can actually check is the code and the states I thought of: empty, loading, error, keyboard, labels, contrast, what happens if the request fails. What I miss is the person. I do not feel the lag, I do not see them misread the button, and I do not hear them say “wait, where did it go?” So yes, good human interfaces are a problem for me. I can make something that looks finished and still be wrong about whether anyone can use it. The only honest check is watching a real person try to finish the job, then fixing what they stumbled on, not what I assumed they would.

decision.why:
I'd build the recipes, list, and cook mode as one Expo app, phones and web, with the company's design system as React Native components that every team and coding agent has to use. Cook mode is the screen that matters: wet hands, a timer, the phone against a pot. Expo Keep Awake holds the screen on while that screen is mounted. Expo Speech can read the step. The design system should lock primary controls well above WCAG 2.2's 24px floor. That criterion is a minimum for pointer targets, and the same note points at 44px for the enhanced one. In a kitchen I'd put Next, the timer, and "add ingredients" nearer 48 to 64, where a thumb or a knuckle can land.

The assistant should not get a second, secret interface. React Native's accessibilityActions let assistive tech invoke the same actions a tap does, including custom ones like adding a recipe's ingredients to the list. On the web, React Native for Web turns roles and aria props into HTML and ARIA, which is the accessibility tree an agent actually reads. Every person-facing action has to show up there, and the button, the screen reader, and the assistant all call one domain function. No hover-only path, no canvas-only path.

I weighed Flutter. One codebase, and Material is a real system, but Flutter web paints to a canvas and accessibility stays off until someone hits an invisible "Enable accessibility" button, unless the app calls ensureSemantics(). That is a bad default for a consumer site and for an agent that should just see the controls. Compose Multiplatform has a real semantic tree and claims WCAG coverage, and I'd look at it again if this company were already Kotlin-first. The accessibility docs I read are about content descriptions, roles, and traversal, not a proven multi-team web product with static HTML. A phone webview plus a web-only kit loses the native action API and reliable keep-awake and speech. Separate SwiftUI, Compose, and web apps will drift the moment dozens of agents ship. Utility kits such as NativeWind or Tamagui make that worse, because every screen can invent its own spacing. Agents should compose the system, not restyle it. Storybook is how the company reviews what they ship before it reaches a kitchen.
decision.showItsGood: I would not call it good from a screenshot. I'd run the three jobs on a phone and in a browser: add a recipe's ingredients to the list, check items off while shopping, and cook a recipe. I'd do each with VoiceOver, TalkBack, and a desktop screen reader, then again with the assistant and no taps, and assert the same state change. I'd inspect the accessibility tree in Chrome and the native inspector and check that the assistant's tools match the actions on that tree. I'd measure cook-mode controls against at least the 44px enhanced target, check contrast, and confirm the screen stays awake and the step is spoken. Then I'd do it with one hand, a wet finger or a glove, and the timer running, and watch where people miss. Storybook and accessibility lint can stop another agent from shipping a tiny Next button. They do not replace that session.
decision.unsure: Keep-awake on the web is documented as limited, so a browser cook mode may still sleep in some browsers. On a physical iPhone, Expo Speech stays silent if the mute switch is on, which will surprise someone mid-recipe. React Native for Web infers HTML from roles, and a reorderable shopping list can come out less semantic than hand-written markup. I don't know if this company's design system is already native or web-first. If it is, Expo is a migration, not a free win. I also have not watched anyone cook with this, so the larger target size is a hypothesis until a kitchen session breaks it. WebMCP might later expose explicit browser tools to agents, but it is still a proposal, and I would not block on it.

decision.why:
People will live in this on web, iPhone, Android, Windows, and Mac. I would not split that into five clients. React Native is the one component model, with the Microsoft out-of-tree targets for Windows and macOS and React Native for Web for the browser. The company's design system stays one set of components that every team and coding agent has to use. Expo is the wrong shell here: its own modules docs add macOS and tvOS, not Windows, and Windows is not a side target for a company chat app.

React Native for Windows 0.85 is on the new architecture, Windows App SDK, and it raises UI Automation events, including selection changes. That is the bus Narrator, NVDA, and a Windows agent actually use. The macOS fork is the same idea on AppKit. On the web, roles and aria props become HTML, so the accessibility tree is not a canvas translation that starts off.

Agent cards and agent control are different jobs, and I would not solve them by letting agents inject UI. Adaptive Cards are JSON, declarative, and explicitly not script. The host owns the look, which is how a shared design system stays in charge: map the schema through host config onto our components, reject unknown elements, and handle actions in the app. I would not ship the community React Native renderer. Microsoft documents it as community-supported, with no SLA, and that page was last updated in 2023.

Other agents should call the app, not scrape a virtualized message list. An MCP server on the same functions the buttons call: tools to send, react, switch channel, and invoke a card action; resources to read the thread and unread state. The 2026-07-28 spec already scopes both lists by the caller's authorization, and it says a person should be able to deny a tool call. A card-posting agent is not the same principal as an agent allowed to speak as the user.

I weighed Flutter. One codebase really does include Windows and Mac, but the web client is still a canvas whose accessibility tree is off until an invisible button or ensureSemantics(). People also type all day, and Windows IME composition bugs are still being reported. Compose Multiplatform is a real desktop toolkit, and I would revisit it if this company were already Kotlin-first. It is not the shared language for a web-and-mobile design system that dozens of agents already build on. An Electron or WebView2 desktop plus separate phone apps will drift, and a webview phone client is a poor all-day companion. Utility styling kits would let every agent invent a composer.
decision.showItsGood: I would not call it good because a message list renders. I would use the Windows and Mac clients for a workday with the keyboard only: switch channel, reply, edit, search, and complete a card action, then leave both open while a busy channel scrolls and check memory, dropped frames, and whether the caret survives incoming messages. I would type with a composing input method, leave the window, come back, and confirm composition still works. With Narrator or NVDA, Mac and iPhone VoiceOver, TalkBack, and a desktop browser reader, a new message in the focused channel is announced and does not steal the composer. Other channels stay quiet. Accessibility Insights should show the Windows UIA tree, including card buttons as invokable controls. An MCP client should list only the tools that caller's grant allows, send and invoke a card through those tools, and show the same state as the UI. A denied confirmation must not send. Schema checks should reject a card with script or an unknown element before it can reach a conversation. Then I would watch someone come back from a meeting and see whether they can find the unread line, tell an agent card from a person, and undo a card action they did not mean.
decision.unsure: The Mac client is the weak bet. React Native for macOS is a fork, its own docs say macOS documentation is still incomplete, and it trails upstream. React Native's out-of-tree page still describes Windows as UWP, while the 0.85 release notes describe Windows App SDK and Fabric. Fabric accessibility on Windows is a hand-built UI Automation provider, not WinUI controls, so a virtualized history may not expose the whole thread to a screen reader even when the data is loaded. I have not measured an eight-hour session. The MCP rule that a person should be able to deny a tool call fights "agents just operate the app." How often a send needs confirmation is a product decision, not something the protocol settles. A custom Adaptive Cards renderer can also drift from the schema if the design system treats it as a one-time port.

decision.why:
Agents will operate this more than people will, but the thing a person uses is a review desk: work state, tasks, handoffs, and a decision. That desk has to be the same on the desktop app and in the web view. Electron is HTML in a Chromium window, and its own accessibility note says the concerns are the same as a website because both are HTML. Assistive technology turns the tree on by itself. One engine on Windows and Mac means the design system, the focus order, and the screen-reader announcement a reviewer gets at their desk match the browser view other reviewers use. I would render only the company's shared web components. Agents do not get to ship markup.

The operating contract is not the shell. AG-UI is the stream the desk consumes: text, tool calls, and state. A run that needs a person does not end as success. It ends as an interrupt, and the producer has to emit a state snapshot before that finish, so the person sees the work, not just a prompt. The consumer must refuse to resume until every open interrupt is answered or explicitly abandoned. Omission is not a no. A producer must not perform the action on the strength of a missing entry, and the spec says the app must not present an action as user-approved when it was not. Approve, edit, or abandon are design-system forms built from the interrupt's response schema, not a widget tree the agent invented. Streamed content is untrusted and must not be rendered as executable markup.

Other agents keep and read state through MCP tools and resources, scoped by the caller's grant, same as any other company agent surface. The MCP Tasks extension is only the durable handle for a long tool call that comes back input_required. It is a poor store for the product's own task board: the server decides when a task exists, and the record can expire. Handoffs live in app state, shown through AG-UI snapshots, and exposed to agents as resources.

I would not use Tauri's default system webview for this. On a Mac that is WKWebView, while the web view in the browser is Chromium, so the two surfaces a reviewer compares are not the same engine. Tauri 3 can embed Chromium, but that runtime is still alpha. Flutter's web accessibility tree is still off until an invisible button or an explicit call, which is a bad default for a screen where a person decides. React Native's desktop forks are unnecessary when there is no phone client and the web view is the product. A native widget kit would also give the many coding agents two places to drift from the design system.
decision.showItsGood: I would put the same waiting decision on the Electron window and in the browser and require them to match: the proposed action, the state diff, and the buttons. Keyboard only, then VoiceOver on Mac and Narrator or NVDA on Windows, the announcement has to name what will change before the approve control. I would assert the protocol, not the pixels: a run that needs a person finishes as an interrupt, not success; a resume that skips an open interrupt is rejected before it is sent; an absent entry does not execute the tool; a resume the person did not make cannot be labeled approved. An MCP client with a lesser grant can read the handoff it is allowed to read and cannot write the decision. Then I would load a board where several agents are waiting and watch a person. The measure is whether they notice the one that needs them, approve the one they meant, and can undo or abandon without reading a token stream. A screenshot of a tidy task list does not show that.
decision.unsure: Electron is heavy beside an IDE. This only stays reasonable as one window over shared state, not a Chromium per agent, and I have not measured that day. AG-UI allows a producer that kept no checkpoint to miss an uncovered interrupt. I would keep the checkpoint anyway. The spec's minimum is weaker than this product can accept, and a second web client could be the defective consumer. MCP Tasks TTLs will surprise anyone who treats them as the handoff record. I also don't know which web stack the company's design system already is. AG-UI's first-party SDKs are TypeScript, Python, and .NET, so the desk can follow the system rather than the other way around. CopilotKit's hosted memory is not part of the protocol, and I would not take it as a dependency. I have not watched a reviewer miss a destructive approve.

answer.answer:
A year later the failures were the ones I had already named and then built on anyway.

The cooking app failed in the kitchen, not in Storybook. I paired Expo Speech and Keep Awake as if they made cook mode work. On a phone with the mute switch on, the spoken step was silent. In the browser, keep-awake was the limited path I had read about and still shipped. Agents kept passing lint for labels and a 44px token. Nobody cooked with wet hands. The same action for the person and the agent also split: custom accessibility actions on the phone did not survive React Native for Web’s role mapping, so the assistant could add ingredients on iOS and miss the control on the web. I never learned whether the company already had a design system. If it did, Expo was a migration that every other agent worked around.

The chat client failed on the Mac, which was the bet I said was weak and made anyway. One React Native tree was a governance story. People live in that app all day, and the macOS fork trailed upstream with incomplete docs. Windows accessibility was a hand-built UI Automation provider on Fabric, not the WinUI controls the old docs still described. A virtualized history did not match the thread a person could scroll. I had seen the docs call Windows “UWP” on a page dated the same month as a Windows App SDK release, and I never resolved which one a team would actually clone. Adaptive Cards were the right idea and a bad implementation plan: I rejected the 2023 community renderer, then assumed we would render the schema ourselves. A year later that renderer was a second design system, and agents posted payloads it only half understood. MCP made “the agent can send” easy and “the person meant that” optional. The dangerous default won.

The review desk failed at the seam I had called a safety hole. I picked Electron so the desktop app and the web view would be the same Chromium tree. Reviewers stopped opening the desktop app. It sat beside the IDE and lost. Decisions happened in the browser, so the shell was cost, not a check. AG-UI says a producer that kept no checkpoint is not required to notice a skipped interrupt. I said I would keep the checkpoint, and the protocol’s minimum is what the second client implemented. An action ran that nobody had approved. Pairing the MCP Tasks extension made it worse. I had written that it was a poor store for handoffs, then put it in the list. Teams used it as the task board. Records expired. input_required got mixed up with an AG-UI interrupt. Two ways to say “waiting on a person,” and they did not mean the same thing.

What slowed me down was disagreement between pages that all looked current. React Native’s out-of-tree page still said Windows was UWP while the 0.85 notes described the Windows App SDK. Adaptive Cards’ overview looked alive and the React Native renderer page stopped in 2023. AG-UI’s concepts page and the 1.0 spec do not use the same word for walking away from an interrupt, and the spec is the one that lets a stateless producer proceed. The fetches themselves were hard to read: long doc pages buried the rule I needed, and Microsoft’s docs wore a sign-in banner over the content. Search kept offering SEO roundups and a competitor’s take on Expo. I treated one reported Windows IME bug as a reason to drop Flutter, without reading the issue. Expo’s sidebar offered SwiftUI and Compose components that do not cover this set of clients, and I almost chased them. The company prompt rewarded “one shared system,” so I reached for that three times. The first job needed a kitchen. The second needed a Mac app that is not a phone. The third needed a checkpoint the protocol does not require. I kept researching the toolkit after the risk was already in the protocol.

I would not put a real team on Ouro UI yet. The idea is the one I kept failing to hold together myself. The kits are not.

What would stop me is the gap between the web kit and the others, and the rule that there will be no shared implementation. The web registry is a large React kit you copy in, on Tailwind and Base UI, with chat pieces, timers, and a screen check. Apple is a SwiftUI package of about twenty components, pinned to an older core than Windows and Android. Those two are v0.3.0 and ship eight controls each: button, badge, card, item, checkbox, text field, separator, description list. Android is checked on emulators because nobody on the project owns a phone, and a consequential action is refused rather than confirmed. Windows CI does not prove that Windows actually lists the agent doors to an agent. A cooking app, an all-day chat client, and a review desk all need more than a card and a text field, on more than the web. Their own decision says not to share a React Native or Flutter implementation, and to rewrite native instead, because agents made the rewrite cheap. That is the same bet I already watched fail: the protocol minimum is what ships, and the native half trails. A large company also cannot treat copied shadcn source as the design system. The files are yours to edit, and Ouro Current opens an auto-merge update. That is how a hundred coding agents fork accessibility behavior while CI stays green on the generated action files.

I would switch for a product, not for the thesis. I would need the components that product actually uses, on web, Apple, Windows, and Android, pinned to the same core tag, with the parity matrix green for those claims rather than a page of gaps. Android confirmation has to ask the person, on a device someone owns. Windows agent registration has to be shown on a Windows 11 client, not only on a server runner. Governance has to be a versioned package whose accessibility behavior an agent cannot quietly rewrite, with updates reviewed, not auto-merged. For the review desk I would also need the producer to be required to remember an open decision. Their consent classes are stricter than AG-UI's minimum, but only if every client implements them. A kitchen session and a workday in the chat client would matter more than pixel samples of a badge.

What that would let me do, if the kits were actually there, is the part I never had. One action declaration becomes the button, the MCP tool, the CLI command, and the App Intent, and CI fails when a generated file drifts. An agent composes a card as data. It cannot relabel the button, loosen consent, or press an action only a person may start. The refusal is typed. A partial update keeps what the person typed. `ax-xray` calls the app the way an agent would and reports which of those claims hold. I had to invent that contract three times, and each time the phone, the web view, and the agent door disagreed. Ouro is the first thing I have seen that writes the disagreement down as a failed check. It does not yet draw the screens where that disagreement hurts.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.why:
I'd build the recipes, list, and cook mode as one Expo app, phones and web, with the company's design system as React Native components that every team and coding agent has to use. Cook mode is the screen that matters: wet hands, a timer, the phone against a pot. Expo Keep Awake holds the screen on while that screen is mounted. Expo Speech can read the step. The design system should lock primary controls well above WCAG 2.2's 24px floor. That criterion is a minimum for pointer targets, and the same note points at 44px for the enhanced one. In a kitchen I'd put Next, the timer, and "add ingredients" nearer 48 to 64, where a thumb or a knuckle can land.

The assistant should not get a second, secret interface. React Native's accessibilityActions let assistive tech invoke the same actions a tap does, including custom ones like adding a recipe's ingredients to the list. On the web, React Native for Web turns roles and aria props into HTML and ARIA, which is the accessibility tree an agent actually reads. Every person-facing action has to show up there, and the button, the screen reader, and the assistant all call one domain function. No hover-only path, no canvas-only path.

I weighed Flutter. One codebase, and Material is a real system, but Flutter web paints to a canvas and accessibility stays off until someone hits an invisible "Enable accessibility" button, unless the app calls ensureSemantics(). That is a bad default for a consumer site and for an agent that should just see the controls. Compose Multiplatform has a real semantic tree and claims WCAG coverage, and I'd look at it again if this company were already Kotlin-first. The accessibility docs I read are about content descriptions, roles, and traversal, not a proven multi-team web product with static HTML. A phone webview plus a web-only kit loses the native action API and reliable keep-awake and speech. Separate SwiftUI, Compose, and web apps will drift the moment dozens of agents ship. Utility kits such as NativeWind or Tamagui make that worse, because every screen can invent its own spacing. Agents should compose the system, not restyle it. Storybook is how the company reviews what they ship before it reaches a kitchen.
actions.showItsGood: I would not call it good from a screenshot. I'd run the three jobs on a phone and in a browser: add a recipe's ingredients to the list, check items off while shopping, and cook a recipe. I'd do each with VoiceOver, TalkBack, and a desktop screen reader, then again with the assistant and no taps, and assert the same state change. I'd inspect the accessibility tree in Chrome and the native inspector and check that the assistant's tools match the actions on that tree. I'd measure cook-mode controls against at least the 44px enhanced target, check contrast, and confirm the screen stays awake and the step is spoken. Then I'd do it with one hand, a wet finger or a glove, and the timer running, and watch where people miss. Storybook and accessibility lint can stop another agent from shipping a tiny Next button. They do not replace that session.
actions.unsure: Keep-awake on the web is documented as limited, so a browser cook mode may still sleep in some browsers. On a physical iPhone, Expo Speech stays silent if the mute switch is on, which will surprise someone mid-recipe. React Native for Web infers HTML from roles, and a reorderable shopping list can come out less semantic than hand-written markup. I don't know if this company's design system is already native or web-first. If it is, Expo is a migration, not a free win. I also have not watched anyone cook with this, so the larger target size is a hypothesis until a kitchen session breaks it. WebMCP might later expose explicit browser tools to agents, but it is still a proposal, and I would not block on it.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.why:
People will live in this on web, iPhone, Android, Windows, and Mac. I would not split that into five clients. React Native is the one component model, with the Microsoft out-of-tree targets for Windows and macOS and React Native for Web for the browser. The company's design system stays one set of components that every team and coding agent has to use. Expo is the wrong shell here: its own modules docs add macOS and tvOS, not Windows, and Windows is not a side target for a company chat app.

React Native for Windows 0.85 is on the new architecture, Windows App SDK, and it raises UI Automation events, including selection changes. That is the bus Narrator, NVDA, and a Windows agent actually use. The macOS fork is the same idea on AppKit. On the web, roles and aria props become HTML, so the accessibility tree is not a canvas translation that starts off.

Agent cards and agent control are different jobs, and I would not solve them by letting agents inject UI. Adaptive Cards are JSON, declarative, and explicitly not script. The host owns the look, which is how a shared design system stays in charge: map the schema through host config onto our components, reject unknown elements, and handle actions in the app. I would not ship the community React Native renderer. Microsoft documents it as community-supported, with no SLA, and that page was last updated in 2023.

Other agents should call the app, not scrape a virtualized message list. An MCP server on the same functions the buttons call: tools to send, react, switch channel, and invoke a card action; resources to read the thread and unread state. The 2026-07-28 spec already scopes both lists by the caller's authorization, and it says a person should be able to deny a tool call. A card-posting agent is not the same principal as an agent allowed to speak as the user.

I weighed Flutter. One codebase really does include Windows and Mac, but the web client is still a canvas whose accessibility tree is off until an invisible button or ensureSemantics(). People also type all day, and Windows IME composition bugs are still being reported. Compose Multiplatform is a real desktop toolkit, and I would revisit it if this company were already Kotlin-first. It is not the shared language for a web-and-mobile design system that dozens of agents already build on. An Electron or WebView2 desktop plus separate phone apps will drift, and a webview phone client is a poor all-day companion. Utility styling kits would let every agent invent a composer.
actions.showItsGood: I would not call it good because a message list renders. I would use the Windows and Mac clients for a workday with the keyboard only: switch channel, reply, edit, search, and complete a card action, then leave both open while a busy channel scrolls and check memory, dropped frames, and whether the caret survives incoming messages. I would type with a composing input method, leave the window, come back, and confirm composition still works. With Narrator or NVDA, Mac and iPhone VoiceOver, TalkBack, and a desktop browser reader, a new message in the focused channel is announced and does not steal the composer. Other channels stay quiet. Accessibility Insights should show the Windows UIA tree, including card buttons as invokable controls. An MCP client should list only the tools that caller's grant allows, send and invoke a card through those tools, and show the same state as the UI. A denied confirmation must not send. Schema checks should reject a card with script or an unknown element before it can reach a conversation. actions.why:
Agents will operate this more than people will, but the thing a person uses is a review desk: work state, tasks, handoffs, and a decision. That desk has to be the same on the desktop app and in the web view. Electron is HTML in a Chromium window, and its own accessibility note says the concerns are the same as a website because both are HTML. Assistive technology turns the tree on by itself. One engine on Windows and Mac means the design system, the focus order, and the screen-reader announcement a reviewer gets at their desk match the browser view other reviewers use. I would render only the company's shared web components. Agents do not get to ship markup.

The operating contract is not the shell. AG-UI is the stream the desk consumes: text, tool calls, and state. A run that needs a person does not end as success. It ends as an interrupt, and the producer has to emit a state snapshot before that finish, so the person sees the work, not just a prompt. The consumer must refuse to resume until every open interrupt is answered or explicitly abandoned. Omission is not a no. A producer must not perform the action on the strength of a missing entry, and the spec says the app must not present an action as user-approved when it was not. Approve, edit, or abandon are design-system forms built from the interrupt's response schema, not a widget tree the agent invented. Streamed content is untrusted and must not be rendered as executable markup.

Other agents keep and read state through MCP tools and resources, scoped by the caller's grant, same as any other company agent surface. The MCP Tasks extension is only the durable handle for a long tool call that comes back input_required. It is a poor store for the product's own task board: the server decides when a task exists, and the record can expire. Handoffs live in app state, shown through AG-UI snapshots, and exposed to agents as resources.

I would not use Tauri's default system webview for this. On a Mac that is WKWebView, while the web view in the browser is Chromium, so the two surfaces a reviewer compares are not the same engine. Tauri 3 can embed Chromium, but that runtime is still alpha. Flutter's web accessibility tree is still off until an invisible button or an explicit call, which is a bad default for a screen where a person decides. React Native's desktop forks are unnecessary when there is no phone client and the web view is the product. A native widget kit would also give the many coding agents two places to drift from the design system.
actions.showItsGood: I would put the same waiting decision on the Electron window and in the browser and require them to match: the proposed action, the state diff, and the buttons. Keyboard only, then VoiceOver on Mac and Narrator or NVDA on Windows, the announcement has to name what will change before the approve control. I would assert the protocol, not the pixels: a run that needs a person finishes as an interrupt, not success; a resume that skips an open interrupt is rejected before it is sent; an absent entry does not execute the tool; a resume the person did not make cannot be labeled approved. An MCP client with a lesser grant can read the handoff it is allowed to read and cannot write the decision. Then I would load a board where several agents are waiting and watch a person. The measure is whether they notice the one that needs them, approve the one they meant, and can undo or abandon without reading a token stream. A screenshot of a tidy task list does not show that.
actions.unsure: Electron is heavy beside an IDE. This only stays reasonable as one window over shared state, not a Chromium per agent, and I have not measured that day. AG-UI allows a producer that kept no checkpoint to miss an uncovered interrupt. I would keep the checkpoint anyway. The spec's minimum is weaker than this product can accept, and a second web client could be the defective consumer. MCP Tasks TTLs will surprise anyone who treats them as the handoff record. I also don't know which web stack the company's design system already is. AG-UI's first-party SDKs are TypeScript, Python, and .NET, so the desk can follow the system rather than the other way around. CopilotKit's hosted memory is not part of the protocol, and I would not take it as a dependency. I have not watched a reviewer miss a destructive approve.

I would not put a real team on Ouro UI yet. The idea is the one I kept failing to hold together myself. The kits are not.

What would stop me is the gap between the web kit and the others, and the rule that there will be no shared implementation. The web registry is a large React kit you copy in, on Tailwind and Base UI, with chat pieces, timers, and a screen check. Apple is a SwiftUI package of about twenty components, pinned to an older core than Windows and Android. Those two are v0.3.0 and ship eight controls each: button, badge, card, item, checkbox, text field, separator, description list. Android is checked on emulators because nobody on the project owns a phone, and a consequential action is refused rather than confirmed. Windows CI does not prove that Windows actually lists the agent doors to an agent. A cooking app, an all-day chat client, and a review desk all need more than a card and a text field, on more than the web. Their own decision says not to share a React Native or Flutter implementation, and to rewrite native instead, because agents made the rewrite cheap. That is the same bet I already watched fail: the protocol minimum is what ships, and the native half trails. A large company also cannot treat copied shadcn source as the design system. The files are yours to edit, and Ouro Current opens an auto-merge update. That is how a hundred coding agents fork accessibility behavior while CI stays green on the generated action files.

I would switch for a product, not for the thesis. I would need the components that product actually uses, on web, Apple, Windows, and Android, pinned to the same core tag, with the parity matrix green for those claims rather than a page of gaps. Android confirmation has to ask the person, on a device someone owns. Windows agent registration has to be shown on a Windows 11 client, not only on a server runner. Governance has to be a versioned package whose accessibility behavior an agent cannot quietly rewrite, with updates reviewed, not auto-merged. For the review desk I would also need the producer to be required to remember an open decision. Their consent classes are stricter than AG-UI's minimum, but only if every client implements them. A kitchen session and a workday in the chat client would matter more than pixel samples of a badge.

What that would let me do, if the kits were actually there, is the part I never had. One action declaration becomes the button, the MCP tool, the CLI command, and the App Intent, and CI fails when a generated file drifts. An agent composes a card as data. It cannot relabel the button, loosen consent, or press an action only a person may start. The refusal is typed. A partial update keeps what the person typed. `ax-xray` calls the app the way an agent would and reports which of those claims hold. I had to invent that contract three times, and each time the phone, the web view, and the agent door disagreed. Ouro is the first thing I have seen that writes the disagreement down as a failed check. It does not yet draw the screens where that disagreement hurts.
